name: Ash Wednesday
description: Lent begins. 40 days of repentance and preparation for Easter.
biblicalBasis: Jesus' teaching on fasting, prayer, and giving in secret: "When you fast, do not look gloomy... but anoint your head and wash your face" (Matt 6:1-18). Joel 2:12-13: "Return to me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning. Tear your hearts, not your garments!" Genesis 3:19: "You are dust, and to dust you shall return."
significance: The ash reminds us of mortality and the seriousness of sin. Fasting is not an outward exercise but an inward turning—Joel insists on tearing the heart, not the clothes. The 40 days reflect Jesus' 40 days in the wilderness, Israel's 40 years in the wilderness, and Moses' 40 days on Sinai. Lent is a practice of letting go and making space for God.
liturgicalContext: Purple color. The ash cross is drawn on the forehead with the words "Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return" or "Repent and believe the gospel." Sundays are not counted in the 40 days because each Sunday is a "little Easter."
history: Ash Wednesday has been known since the 600s. Originally, public sinners were assigned penance with ash and sackcloth. Over time, the ash cross was given to all believers as a sign of shared confession of sin. Luther retained Ash Wednesday as a valuable practice of repentance.
otConnections: Jonah 3:5-10 where the Ninevites fast in sackcloth and ash, and God turns from His wrath. Daniel 9:3 where Daniel prays with fasting, sackcloth, and ash. Job 42:6: "Therefore I despise myself and repent in dust and ash." Esther 4:1-3 where Mordecai's fasting in sackcloth and ash leads to deliverance.

references.reason: The day is defined by Jesus' teaching on fasting, prayer, and giving in secret (Matt 6:1-18). This text is the central Bible passage for the beginning of Lent and reminds us that piety should not be an outward exercise to be seen by others, but an inward turning to God.
